6060:
To "feel it in one's bones" means to have a very strong inner sense or gut feeling that something is true or that something is about to happen — even when you have no logical proof or solid evidence to support it.

It is a deep, instinctive kind of knowing. The feeling comes from somewhere inside you, not from facts, data, or reasoning. You simply know something, and you are so sure of it that it feels almost physical — as if your own body is confirming it.
A Simple Example to Understand It Instantly

Imagine it is a bright, sunny morning. No clouds in the sky, and the weather forecast says it will be a fine day. But you step outside, and something just feels off. You cannot explain it, but deep inside, you are certain it is going to rain. You tell your friend:

"I don't care what the forecast says — I can feel it in my bones. It's going to rain today."

You have no scientific evidence. But your inner sense is so strong that you trust it completely. That is exactly what this idiom captures.
Breaking Down the Words

The idiom refers to your bones — the deepest, hardest parts of your body. Bones are hidden deep inside, beneath your skin and muscles. Choosing "bones" to describe this feeling is very deliberate and meaningful:

  • It means the feeling is not shallow or surface-level.
  • It is buried deep within you, at your very core.
  • It is not a small, uncertain whisper. It is a strong, solid, unshakeable sense.

So when you "feel something in your bones," it means the feeling is not just in your head or your heart — it goes all the way to the deepest part of you.
Where Did This Idiom Come From?

The origin of this phrase is rooted in a very old, widespread belief that human bones can sense changes in the weather.

For centuries, people — especially the elderly and those with joint pain or arthritis — would experience aching or throbbing in their bones before a storm, rain, or cold spell. The change in air pressure before bad weather genuinely does affect joints and bones for many people. So a grandmother might say:

"My bones are aching — a storm is coming."

Over time, this very real, physical experience of bones "predicting" something that was about to happen became a metaphor for intuition in general. People started applying it beyond just weather, using it to describe any strong inner prediction or certainty about life events. The idiom has been in English use for several centuries and appears in literature as far back as the 1500s.
The Full Emotional Weight of This Idiom

This idiom is not used for weak, uncertain guesses. It is used when someone feels:

  • Completely sure, not just slightly confident.
  • Emotionally charged about what they sense.
  • Unable to explain the feeling logically, yet unwilling to dismiss it.

It sits in the space between logic and instinct — closer to instinct. It is what you might call a "beyond doubt" gut feeling.
How to Use It in a Sentence

Here are natural, everyday examples showing how the idiom is used:

  1. Positive prediction:

    "I feel it in my bones — our team is going to win the championship this year."

  2. Negative premonition:

    "Something is wrong. I feel it in my bones."

  3. Certainty about a person:

    "I've never even met him, but I feel it in my bones that he can't be trusted."

  4. Certainty about an outcome:

    "She felt it in her bones that the job offer was coming, even before the phone rang."

  5. Casual everyday use:

    "Don't ask me how I know — I just feel it in my bones."
The Grammar of the Idiom

It is helpful to know the different ways this idiom can be structured:

  • "I feel it in my bones" — present tense, current feeling.
  • "I felt it in my bones" — past tense, describing a past premonition.
  • "I can feel it in my bones" — emphasizing the strength of the feeling right now.
  • "I knew it in my bones" — past tense, often said after the premonition turned out to be correct.
  • "Something in my bones tells me..." — a variation that flows naturally in conversation.
What This Idiom Is NOT

It is important to understand what this phrase does not mean:

  • It does not mean you have a logical argument or evidence.
  • It does not mean you have pain in your literal bones.
  • It does not mean a casual guess or a weak suspicion — it always carries a sense of deep certainty.
  • It does not mean you looked something up or were told by someone else. The certainty comes entirely from within you.
Similar Idioms and Expressions

If you understand "feel it in one's bones," you will also immediately understand these closely related expressions:

  • "A gut feeling" — an instinctive feeling originating from deep inside (the gut/stomach area), similar in meaning.
  • "A sixth sense" — an almost supernatural inner awareness beyond the five regular senses.
  • "I have a hunch" — a softer, slightly less certain version of the same idea.
  • "Something tells me..." — a vague inner voice pointing toward something.
  • "I sense it in my blood" — a rarer but similar phrase emphasizing deep, inherited intuition.

Among all of these, "feel it in one's bones" is one of the strongest and most emphatic, because bones are so deep and solid. It conveys more certainty than "a hunch" or "something tells me."
Tone and Register — When Is It Used?

This idiom is:

  • Informal to neutral in tone — perfectly suitable in casual conversation, storytelling, or informal writing.
  • Not rude or offensive in any context.
  • Not formal — you would not typically use it in a business report or academic essay, but it is absolutely fine in speeches, novels, conversations, and everyday writing.
  • Very common in spoken English across British, American, Australian, and other varieties of English worldwide.
One Final Way to Remember It Forever

Think of it this way:

Your skin feels things on the surface. Your heart feels emotions. But your bones — hidden deep inside, holding your whole body together — they feel the things that go beyond ordinary sensation. When something reaches all the way to your bones, it is as deep and certain as anything can possibly get.

That is why when you "feel it in your bones," it means your certainty is not just skin-deep. It is at your very core.
6061:
To feel sorry for oneself means to spend too much time pitying yourself over your own problems, bad luck, or suffering — often in a way that others (or even you yourself) consider excessive, unproductive, or self-indulgent.

It is not just about feeling sad. It is specifically about focusing deeply and repeatedly on your own misfortune, often without doing anything to fix it.

Think of it this way: if a friend loses their job and spends the next three months lying in bed, complaining all day, refusing to try again, and constantly thinking "Why does this always happen to ME?" — that person is feeling sorry for themselves.

Normally, we "feel sorry for" other people. For example:

"I feel sorry for him — he lost everything in the fire."

This is normal sympathy. You are feeling pity toward someone else's suffering.

But when you turn that pity inward — toward yourself — and you do it excessively, it becomes "feeling sorry for oneself."

"Stop feeling sorry for yourself and do something about it!"

The word "oneself" signals that the pity is completely self-directed and self-absorbed.

This idiom is almost always negative. It carries a tone of mild criticism or disapproval. When someone tells you to stop feeling sorry for yourself, they are essentially saying:

  • You are dwelling on your pain too much.
  • You are not being productive.
  • You are exaggerating your suffering, or at least not handling it well.
  • It is time to move forward.

It implies that the person has crossed the line from understandable sadness into something more like wallowing — swimming around in their own unhappiness without trying to swim out.
The Difference Between Normal Sadness and Feeling Sorry for Yourself

This is an important distinction many learners miss.

Feeling sad, upset, or hurt after something bad happens is completely normal and healthy. If you fail an important exam, feeling disappointed is natural. If someone you love leaves you, feeling heartbroken is human.

But feeling sorry for yourself is what happens when you stay stuck in that pain for too long, you keep replaying it, you focus entirely on yourself and your misfortune, and — crucially — you make no effort to move on or improve things. There is often a sense of "Why me? I don't deserve this!" running underneath it.

The line between the two is crossed when the feeling becomes more about dramatic self-focus than genuine processing of pain.
Common Situations Where This Idiom Is Used

You will hear this idiom in three main ways:

1. As advice or a warning to someone else (usually sharp in tone)

"You failed the test. Now stop feeling sorry for yourself and study harder next time."

"There's no use in feeling sorry for yourself. Life goes on."

2. As a self-aware observation about your own behavior

"I know I've just been sitting here feeling sorry for myself, but I need to get up and fix this."

"After the breakup, I spent a week feeling sorry for myself, and then I decided to move on."

3. As a gentle or firm piece of advice from someone who cares about you

"I understand you're hurting, but you can't just keep feeling sorry for yourself forever, sweetheart."

When someone is feeling sorry for themselves, there is usually a mix of these emotions going on:

  • Self-pity (thinking your suffering is uniquely terrible)
  • Helplessness (feeling like you cannot change the situation)
  • Resentment (feeling it is unfair that this happened to you)
  • Inaction (not trying to fix or change anything)

The idiom captures all of these at once in just four words, which is what makes it so efficient and powerful.

These phrases are close relatives of "feel sorry for oneself" — knowing them will help you see the full picture:

"Wallow in self-pity" — very similar in meaning, but even stronger. To wallow means to roll around in something (like a pig in mud). So "wallowing in self-pity" suggests you are rolling around in your own misery, enjoying it in an unhealthy way.

"Throw yourself a pity party" — a sarcastic, informal expression. A "pity party" is an imaginary party where the only guest is you, and the only activity is feeling bad for yourself. People use this to gently or not-so-gently mock excessive self-pity.

"Lick your wounds" — similar but slightly more neutral or even sympathetic. It suggests you are recovering quietly from a defeat or injury. Unlike "feeling sorry for yourself," it does not always carry harsh criticism.

Do not confuse "feeling sorry for yourself" with genuine grief, depression, or emotional processing. This idiom is specifically about self-pity that others (or you yourself) recognize as excessive or unproductive. It is not a clinical term, and it should never be used to dismiss someone who is genuinely struggling with serious mental or emotional health issues. Context and tone always matter.

To feel sorry for oneself = to focus excessively on your own suffering, bad luck, or problems in a self-pitying way, usually without doing anything constructive about it. The idiom carries a negative tone and suggests it is time to stop dwelling and start moving forward.

A simple memory trick: imagine someone sitting alone in a corner, head down, muttering "Poor me... why does this always happen to me?" — that image is the heart of this idiom.
6062:
To feel sorry for someone means to feel sadness, sympathy, or compassion in your heart because someone else is suffering, struggling, or in an unfortunate situation.

You are not the one going through the pain — but when you see or hear about their pain, something inside you aches for them. That emotional response is what this expression captures.

"I feel sorry for the children who lost their homes in the flood."
(You are safe, but their suffering touches your heart.)
Breaking It Down Word by Word

Even though this is a fixed expression, understanding each word helps you feel its full weight.

Feel — This is about an emotion, not a thought. It lives in your heart, not your head. You don't think sorry for someone — you feel it.

Sorry — In this context, "sorry" does not mean apologising. It means feeling sadness or grief because of something. The word "sorry" comes from an old English word meaning grief-stricken or pained — so "feel sorry" literally means "feel grief."

For someone — This tiny word "for" is very important. It tells you the emotion is directed outward — toward another person. You are not hurting yourself; you are emotionally responding to someone else's situation.

When you feel sorry for someone, you experience a mix of:

  • Sadness — their situation makes you unhappy
  • Compassion — you genuinely care about their wellbeing
  • Helplessness — often, you wish you could fix things for them but may not be able to
  • Empathy — you can imagine how painful or difficult their situation must be

It is a warm, human emotion. It shows that you are not indifferent to another person's suffering.
The Hidden Layer: Pity vs. Compassion

This is one of the most important and subtle things to understand about this expression.

"Feel sorry for someone" sits right at the boundary between two feelings: compassion and pity. And depending on the context and tone, it can lean either way.

When it leans toward compassion:
You genuinely care. You feel sad with the person. There is warmth and humanity in it.

"I feel so sorry for Maria — she has been working three jobs just to pay her rent."

When it leans toward pity:
You feel sorry for someone from a position of superiority — as if you are looking down at them. This can sometimes feel slightly cold or condescending, even if not intended that way.

"I feel sorry for people who have never read a good book in their life."
(Here the speaker sounds as if they pity those people from a higher level.)

This is why in real life, sometimes people say: "Don't feel sorry for me — I don't need your pity." They are rejecting the slightly condescending version of the feeling.

The key takeaway: the expression itself is neutral — it is the tone and context that determines whether it sounds like warm compassion or cold pity.
"Feel Sorry FOR Someone" vs. "Feel Sorry ABOUT Something"

This is a very common point of confusion for learners. The preposition changes the entire meaning.

Feel sorry FOR someone = You feel sympathy toward a person because of their situation.

"I feel sorry for him — he lost his job yesterday."
(Your emotion is directed at the person.)

Feel sorry ABOUT something = You feel regret or guilt about an event or action.

"I feel sorry about what I said to you last night."
(You regret something that happened.)

Think of it this way:

  • FOR a person → sympathy / compassion / pity
  • ABOUT something → regret / guilt
"Feel Sorry For Someone" vs. "Feel Sorry For Yourself"

When you turn the expression inward — toward yourself — the meaning changes completely.

"Feel sorry for yourself" means to dwell in self-pity. You focus excessively on your own misfortune, often in a way that others find unproductive or dramatic.

It is almost always used in a negative or critical way:

"Stop feeling sorry for yourself and do something about it."
"There's no use sitting around feeling sorry for yourself."

This is a fixed, well-known phrase that carries a clear message: self-pity is a trap — get up and take action.

So remember:

  • Feel sorry for someone else = compassion (generally positive)
  • Feel sorry for yourself = self-pity (generally negative)
How It Is Used in Real Life

In everyday speech:

"I feel so sorry for her — she's been sick all month."
"Don't you feel sorry for the dog left out in the rain?"

In news and discussion:

"Many people feel sorry for the victims of the earthquake."

In advice:

"It's okay to feel sorry for someone, but don't let it become pity that makes them feel weak."

As a rejection of pity:

"You don't have to feel sorry for me. I'm doing just fine."

This phrase is:

  • Informal to neutral in tone — perfectly natural in everyday conversation, writing, news, and literature
  • Suitable for both spoken and written English
  • Used across all ages and contexts

"Feel sorry for someone" means to feel sadness and compassion in your heart because someone else is in pain, difficulty, or misfortune — and depending on the tone, it can reflect either genuine warmth or a slight sense of pity from above.
6063:
A feeling is something that happens inside you — in your mind, your body, or both. It is a private, inner experience. No one else can directly see or touch your feeling; only you can experience it from the inside.

The word "feeling" covers several related but distinct types of inner experiences. Understanding each one will give you a complete picture.

1. An emotion

This is the most common meaning. A feeling is an emotional state — something that affects your mood and how you experience life at a given moment.

Examples of feelings in this sense: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, love, loneliness, pride, shame, excitement, guilt, jealousy.

"She had a strong feeling of love for her children."
"He couldn't shake the feeling of sadness after the news."

The key thing about an emotion-feeling is that it is not a physical sensation (like pain or heat) — it lives in the emotional or psychological part of your inner world.

2. A physical sensation

A feeling can also be what your body senses — something you physically experience through your skin, muscles, nerves, or organs.

"I love the feeling of warm sand under my feet."
"There was a burning feeling in his throat."
"She felt a feeling of heaviness in her legs after the long run."

Here, "feeling" simply means: the experience of a physical sensation. It is what it feels like — from the inside — to be touched, to be in pain, to feel cold, to feel full after a meal, and so on.

3. A vague inner sense or intuition ("a gut feeling")

Sometimes you sense that something is true or will happen — not because you have clear evidence or logical proof, but just because something inside you hints at it. This is also called a feeling.

"I have a feeling that it's going to rain today."
"She had a feeling that something was wrong, even though no one had told her anything."
"I can't explain it, but I have a feeling we've met before."

This kind of feeling is a hunch — an instinct, an inner impression. It is neither a pure emotion nor a physical sensation. It is more like a quiet signal that your mind sends you, often without a clear reason.

The phrase "gut feeling" comes from this meaning — the idea that this inner sense feels like it comes from your gut (your stomach area), not from careful thinking.

4. An opinion or personal view

When someone asks "What are your feelings on this?", they are asking for your personal opinion or attitude about something — what you think and how you feel about it emotionally.

"My feeling is that we should take more time before deciding."
"What are your feelings about moving to a new city?"

Here, "feeling" is very close in meaning to "opinion" or "view," but with an extra layer — it also captures your emotional reaction, not just your intellectual conclusion. You are sharing what you think AND feel at the same time.

5. The ability or capacity to feel — sensitivity

"Feeling" can also refer to the general capacity a person has to experience emotion, to be moved, to be sensitive.

"She plays the violin with incredible feeling." (She puts deep emotion into her playing.)
"He spoke without feeling — his voice was flat and cold." (He showed no emotional sensitivity.)
"The poem is full of feeling." (The poem is emotionally rich and expressive.)

When someone says an artist, a speaker, or a performer shows "great feeling," they mean the person brings genuine emotion and depth to what they do — they are not just technically doing something; they are living it emotionally.

The absence of feeling is also important: someone who seems cold, unaffected, or indifferent is said to have "no feeling" or to show "a lack of feeling."

6. An atmosphere or mood that something gives off

A place, a piece of music, a painting, or a moment can have a certain "feeling" — meaning the overall impression or emotional quality it gives to the person experiencing it.

"The old house had a feeling of mystery about it."
"The music had a melancholic feeling."
"There was a feeling of tension in the room."

Here, "feeling" refers not to your personal emotional state, but to the emotional tone radiating from something outside you — the mood or character that something seems to carry or project.

Both forms are used, but there is a subtle difference worth knowing.

"A feeling" (singular) often refers to one specific, identifiable experience:

"I had a feeling of dread."

"Feelings" (plural) usually refers to emotions in general, or to the emotional inner life of a person as a whole:

"You hurt my feelings." (You caused me emotional pain.)
"Talk about your feelings." (Express your emotional inner world.)
"She kept her feelings to herself." (She did not share her emotions with others.)

The phrase "hurt someone's feelings" is especially common and important. It means you said or did something that caused that person emotional pain — not physical pain, but the pain of feeling disrespected, dismissed, embarrassed, or unloved.

All these uses of "feeling" share one common thread: something is happening inside a person, and that something is experienced privately, from within.

Whether it is an emotion, a bodily sensation, a hunch, an opinion colored by emotion, the capacity to be emotionally moved, or the mood you perceive in something around you — in every case, "feeling" points to the inner, subjective, lived experience of a human being.

This is what separates a "feeling" from, say, a "fact." A fact exists in the world outside of you and can be verified by others. A feeling exists inside you and can only truly be known by you.

• "I know the feeling" — I understand what you are going through because I have experienced something similar.
  • "Mixed feelings" — having both positive and negative emotions about the same thing at the same time. ("I have mixed feelings about leaving my job — I'm excited but also scared.")
  • "A sense of feeling" / "gut feeling" — an intuition, an inner hunch.
  • "Get a feeling for something" — to gradually begin to understand or become familiar with something through experience. ("After a few weeks, I started to get a feeling for how the job works.")
  • "No hard feelings" — said after a disagreement or conflict to signal that you are not holding a grudge — you are not angry or resentful.
  • "Feelings run high" — people feel very strongly and emotionally about something, often to a point where it could cause conflict.

As a noun, "feeling" is a broad and flexible word that describes your inner, subjective experience — whether that is an emotion (joy, fear, sadness), a physical sensation (warmth, pain), an intuition (a hunch), a personal view with emotional weight (an opinion), the capacity for emotional depth (sensitivity), or the mood you perceive in something around you (an atmosphere). The common thread across all these senses is that a feeling is something experienced from the inside — private, personal, and uniquely yours.
6064:
To feign something means to pretend that you feel, experience, or have something — when you actually don't. You are creating a false impression in someone else's mind by putting on an act.

The key idea is deliberate deception. When you feign something, you know the truth, but you are consciously choosing to display something different on the outside to mislead someone.
Breaking It Down With a Simple Example

Imagine you are at school. Your teacher announces a surprise test. You haven't studied at all. So you suddenly hold your stomach, make a pained face, and tell the teacher you feel sick — even though you feel perfectly fine.

You have just feigned illness.

You weren't sick. But you performed sickness convincingly enough to make someone believe you were. That act of deliberate, conscious performance is exactly what "feign" means.
What Kinds of Things Can You Feign?

This is important: "feign" almost always applies to internal, invisible things — feelings, emotions, mental states, physical conditions, and knowledge (or the lack of it). You fake something that exists inside you, so that others believe your inside matches what you're showing on the outside.

Here are the most natural things people feign:

Emotions and reactions:

  • Feign surprise — pretend to be shocked when you already knew the news
  • Feign happiness — smile and act cheerful when you are actually sad or upset
  • Feign interest — act as though you find something fascinating when you are completely bored
  • Feign indifference — act like you don't care about something you actually care about deeply
  • Feign anger — act furious when you're not really upset at all

Physical conditions:

  • Feign illness — pretend to be sick when you're not
  • Feign sleep — pretend to be asleep when you're awake
  • Feign death — act as though you are dead (this is famously what some animals do in the wild to escape predators)
  • Feign injury — pretend to be hurt when you're fine

Mental states and knowledge:

  • Feign ignorance — pretend you don't know something when you actually do
  • Feign innocence — act as if you had no involvement in something you were actually part of
  • Feign confidence — appear bold and sure of yourself when you are actually terrified inside
The Most Important Nuance: It Is Always Deliberate

"Feign" is never accidental. When you feign something, you are making a choice to deceive. You know the real truth, and you are intentionally hiding it behind a performance.

This is what separates feigning from simply being wrong about how you feel. If someone thinks they're fine but they're actually sick, they aren't feigning health — they're just mistaken. Feigning requires full awareness and intention.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Pretend is the closest word to feign, and in most situations they are interchangeable. However, "feign" carries a stronger sense of a polished, deliberate, and somewhat calculated performance. It often implies that the person is quite skilled at the act of deceiving. "Pretend" is broader and can be innocent (like a child pretending to be a superhero), whereas "feign" almost always implies deception toward another person with something at stake.

Fake is more casual and everyday. You'd say "he faked a smile" in everyday speech; "he feigned a smile" sounds more formal and literary.

Simulate means to imitate or reproduce something — often used in technical or scientific contexts (like a computer simulating weather). It doesn't necessarily involve deceiving a person the way "feign" does.

So among all these words, "feign" is the most deliberate, personal, and deception-focused one.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Feign" is a somewhat formal and literary word. You'll encounter it often in novels, serious writing, journalism, and formal speech. In casual everyday conversation, people tend to use "fake" or "pretend" instead. But you will absolutely encounter "feign" in things you read, and it sounds natural and sophisticated when you use it in writing.

Every time you see or use "feign," the mental picture to hold is this: a person who knows the true reality inside them, but puts on a convincing outward show of something entirely different — on purpose, to deceive someone.

The student feigns illness to avoid the test. The spy feigns ignorance to avoid suspicion. The poker player feigns confidence to bluff their opponent. The heartbroken person feigns happiness so their friends don't worry. In every case, the outside performance is a lie, the person knows it's a lie, and the goal is to make someone else believe the lie.

That is feigning — conscious, deliberate, skilled pretense of an inner state.
6065:
Feigned means deliberately pretended or consciously faked. When something is feigned, it is not real — but crucially, the person showing it knows it isn't real. They are putting on a performance, creating a false impression on purpose.

Think of an actor on stage crying. The tears may look real, but the sadness is feigned — performed intentionally, not felt genuinely.
The Two Things That Make Something "Feigned"

For something to be feigned, two things must be true at the same time:

  1. It is not real. The emotion, reaction, or condition being shown does not actually exist inside the person.
  2. It is deliberate. The person is consciously choosing to display it. This is not a mistake or a misunderstanding — it is an intentional act.

This is what makes "feigned" a precise and strong word. It does not just mean "false." It means knowingly and purposefully false.
What Kinds of Things Can Be "Feigned"?

Feigned is almost always used to describe things that a person performs or displays — typically emotions, reactions, mental states, or physical conditions. You would not say "a feigned diamond" the way you might say "a fake diamond." Feigned applies to human behaviour and expression.

Here are the most common things described as feigned:

Emotions: feigned surprise, feigned sadness, feigned anger, feigned joy
Mental states: feigned interest, feigned enthusiasm, feigned concern, feigned indifference
Social qualities: feigned modesty, feigned innocence, feigned confidence
Physical conditions: feigned illness, feigned sleep, feigned injury

These examples will help you see exactly how the word is used in real life.

  • "Her feigned surprise didn't fool anyone — we all knew she had organised the party herself."

Here, she acted surprised, but she wasn't. She chose to perform surprise.

  • "He listened to the long speech with feigned interest, nodding politely while thinking about something else entirely."

He looked interested. He was not. He faked it deliberately to seem polite.

  • "The soldier's feigned surrender was a trap — the moment the enemy came close, the ambush began."

The surrender was staged on purpose to deceive.

  • "She accepted the compliment with feigned modesty, though everyone could see she was secretly pleased."

She pretended not to care about the praise while actually caring very much.

  • "The child's feigned illness didn't work on his mother, who had seen that trick too many times before."

The child pretended to be sick to avoid school — a conscious, deliberate act.

Understanding why people feign things will help you recognise the word in any context. The reasons vary widely:

  • To be polite: Feigning interest in a boring topic so as not to offend someone.
  • To gain an advantage: Feigning illness to skip school or work, or feigning weakness in a competition.
  • To protect someone: Feigning happiness so that a loved one doesn't worry.
  • To deceive an enemy: In war or conflict, feigning retreat or surrender as a strategy.
  • In performance: Actors, dancers, and storytellers feign emotions as part of their craft — though here, no one is truly being deceived since the audience knows it's a performance.

Notice that feigning is not always morally wrong. It depends entirely on the intention behind it.

This is where many learners get confused, so pay close attention.

Feigned vs. Fake
"Fake" is a broader, more casual word. You can call an object fake (a fake passport, fake gold). "Feigned" is reserved for human performances — emotions, reactions, states. Also, "fake" doesn't always imply deliberate intent, while "feigned" always does.

Feigned vs. False
"False" simply means not true or not real (a false statement, a false alarm). It carries no sense of performance or intent. "Feigned" always involves a person actively performing something they know to be untrue.

Feigned vs. Insincere
"Insincere" means not genuinely meaning what you say or show. It is close to "feigned" in meaning, but softer and less vivid. "Feigned" paints a stronger, more deliberate picture — it emphasises the act of pretending, not just the absence of sincerity.

Feigned vs. Pretended
These are nearly identical in meaning, and can often be used interchangeably. However, "feigned" tends to sound more formal and literary, and carries a slightly stronger sense of skilled or calculated performance. "Pretended" is more everyday.
Words That Mean the Same Thing (Synonyms)

If you ever want to replace "feigned" with another word, these work well:
pretended, simulated, fake, artificial, put-on, sham, manufactured, mock, insincere, hollow
genuine, real, sincere, authentic, heartfelt, true, honest, natural

"Feigned" is not a neutral word. When you describe something as feigned, you are exposing a gap — the gap between what someone is showing and what they are actually feeling. It carries a subtle sense of revelation, as if you are seeing through a performance. This is why it often appears in writing to create dramatic irony, where the reader knows the truth even when other characters do not.
One Line to Remember It Forever

Feigned = deliberately pretending something you know is not true, in order to create a false impression.

If you keep that sentence in your mind, you will never misuse or misunderstand this word.
6066:
A feint is a deliberate, deceptive movement or action made to trick an opponent into thinking you are about to do one thing — so that you can actually do something else.

It is a fake move with a real purpose.

Here is what makes a feint different from a random fake or a simple lie:

A feint is specifically designed to provoke a reaction. You don't just want your opponent to believe something false — you want them to move based on that false belief. And the moment they move in the wrong direction, they have opened themselves up. That opening is what you were after the whole time.

So a feint has two parts:

  • The false move — what you show your opponent
  • The real move — what you were always planning to do

The false move is the bait. The real move is the trap springing shut.

In boxing: A boxer quickly dips his shoulder and shifts his body as if he is about to throw a punch at your stomach. You drop your arms to protect your body. In that split second, he throws a real punch — straight at your face, which is now completely unguarded. The initial move toward your stomach was the feint.

In football / soccer: A forward is running with the ball toward a defender. He shifts his body sharply to the left, as if he is about to go that way. The defender lunges left to block him. The forward cuts right and runs past him clean. That leftward body movement was the feint.

In military strategy: An army launches a loud, aggressive attack on the enemy's eastern flank. The enemy, believing this is the main attack, rushes its soldiers to defend the east. Meanwhile, the army's real, full-scale invasion comes quietly from the west, where defenses are now thin. The eastern attack was a feint — a "diversionary attack" designed to pull the enemy the wrong way.

In fencing: A fencer thrusts their sword toward their opponent's left shoulder. The opponent raises their sword to block the left. The fencer then redirects and strikes the right side, which is now exposed. That initial thrust was the feint.

In everyday conversation: A negotiator says, "We're prepared to walk away from this deal entirely," suggesting they don't care about reaching an agreement. The other party, worried, quickly offers better terms. The negotiator never intended to walk away — that statement was a feint designed to win a concession.

A feint only works if your opponent believes it and reacts to it. If they don't react, the feint fails — there is no opening created.

This is why a good feint has to look completely real. It needs to be convincing enough that your opponent's instincts take over and they commit to their reaction before they can think twice. The deeper the commitment, the better the feint worked.

There is also a timing element: the real move must come immediately after the opponent reacts to the false move, before they can correct themselves.

Understanding what a feint isn't sharpens your understanding of what it is:

  • It is not just a lie or a bluff. A bluff is verbal — you say something false. A feint is a physical or tactical action — you do something false. A poker player who says "I have a great hand" when he doesn't is bluffing. A boxer who fakes a body shot is throwing a feint.
  • It is not a distraction. A distraction simply pulls someone's attention elsewhere. A feint goes further — it deliberately pulls your opponent into making a wrong move, a committed physical or strategic reaction, not just a glance in the wrong direction.
  • It is not an accident. A feint is always intentional. The person making it knows exactly what they're doing. There is strategy and calculation behind it.
Where You Will Encounter This Word

You will most commonly see feint used in:

  • Combat sports (boxing, fencing, wrestling, martial arts)
  • Team sports (football, basketball, rugby)
  • Military history and strategy
  • Chess and competitive games (sometimes, more loosely)
  • Politics and negotiation (when describing tactical maneuvering)
One Final Way to Lock It In

Think of it this way: a feint is when you make your opponent answer a question you never actually asked — and the moment they answer it, you ask the real question. They've already used up their answer.
6067:
To feint means to make a fake move on purpose to trick someone, so that while they react to the fake, you do what you actually intended to do. It is a deliberate act of misdirection — you make your opponent look the wrong way, move the wrong way, or prepare for the wrong thing, and then you strike where they are now vulnerable.

The key ingredient is intention. A feint is never accidental. You plan it. You want your opponent to believe something false, react to it, and in doing so, open themselves up.

Imagine two people arm-wrestling. Before gripping hands, one person suddenly jerks their shoulder as if they're about to lunge forward aggressively. The other person tenses up and leans back to brace. But the first person never actually lunged — they just pretended to. That fake shoulder movement was a feint. The real goal was to make the opponent shift their weight, because now they're off-balance and easier to overpower.

The fake move served one purpose: to make the opponent respond to something that wasn't real, so you could take advantage of their response.
Where You'll See This Word Used

1. Boxing and Martial Arts
This is the most classic setting for "feint." A boxer feints a jab at the opponent's face — pulling back the fist slightly, making the shoulder dip — just enough to make the opponent raise their guard to protect their face. The moment the opponent's guard goes up, the boxer throws a real punch at the now-exposed body. The jab never came. It was a feint.

2. Football, Basketball, and Soccer
A footballer running with the ball feints left — dropping the shoulder, shifting body weight — tricking the defender into sliding or stepping left. Then the footballer cuts right and dashes past. The defender committed to stopping a move that never happened.

3. Military Strategy
An army feints an attack on the eastern border, sending a small force there to make a lot of noise, fire, and movement. The enemy rushes their troops to the east to defend. Meanwhile, the army's main and much larger force quietly attacks from the north, where there are now far fewer defenders. The eastern attack was a feint — never the real target.

4. Everyday Life
Though less common, you can use it informally. If someone is about to grab the TV remote from you and you move your hand left to make them reach left, then grab the remote with your right hand, you feinted.
The Exact Mechanism — Break It Down

A feint always has three moving parts:

  1. The fake signal — you do something (a movement, an action, sometimes even words) that your opponent reads as your real intention.
  2. The opponent's reaction — they believe the signal and respond to it. They move, they adjust, they commit.
  3. Your real move — because they've now reacted and shifted, a gap or weakness has opened up. You exploit it.

Remove any one of these three parts, and it's no longer really a feint. If the opponent doesn't react, the feint failed. If you had no real follow-up move planned, it wasn't a feint — it was just a random fake.
What Makes a Feint Different from Simply "Faking"

The word fake is broad and casual. You can fake a smile, fake an illness, fake a document. "Fake" just means something isn't genuine.

Feint is narrower and sharper. It almost always refers to physical or tactical misdirection in a contest or conflict — a fight, a game, a battle. And it specifically implies that the fake is designed to cause the opponent to move or commit in the wrong direction, creating an opening. There is always a strategic purpose behind a feint: to produce a specific reaction from the opponent that you then exploit.

Think of it this way: all feints involve faking, but not all faking is feinting.

• The fencer feinted toward her opponent's left shoulder, and the moment he raised his sword to block, she thrust low and won the point.
  • He feinted right, watched the goalkeeper dive that way, then calmly rolled the ball into the left corner.
  • The general feinted an assault on the bridge to pull the enemy forces away from the hill.
  • She feinted toward the cookie jar so her little brother would rush over, then snatched the TV remote behind him.
One-Line Summary to Lock It In

To feint is to deliberately make a convincing fake move in order to trick an opponent into reacting to it, so that you can then make your real, effective move against the opening their reaction creates.
6068:
Feisty describes someone who is full of energy, spirit, and fight — someone who is bold, loud, and refuses to back down, especially when you might not expect it from them.

Think of a tiny dog that barks fearlessly at a dog ten times its size. Or a small, elderly woman who gives sharp, witty replies to anyone who tries to dismiss her. That boldness, that "I won't be pushed around" energy — that's feisty.
What It Really Means (Layer by Layer)

Feisty has three qualities packed into one word:

1. Energetic and lively. A feisty person is never quiet, dull, or passive. They are animated, spirited, and full of life.

2. Quick to argue or fight back. They don't stay silent when challenged. They speak up, push back, and defend themselves or their views with sharp words and confidence.

3. Not easily intimidated. A feisty person doesn't shrink when faced with opposition, criticism, or someone more powerful. They hold their ground.

The key ingredient that makes feisty special is contrast. The word is most commonly used when the person (or animal) seems like they shouldn't be so bold — because they're small, young, old, outnumbered, or in a weaker position — but they are anyway. That unexpected fighting spirit is the heart of the word.
Who or What Can Be Feisty?

People: This is the most common use. It can describe a child who boldly talks back, a short person who never lets their size make them feel small, an elderly person who is surprisingly sharp and spirited, or anyone who argues with passion and doesn't accept being pushed around.

Animals: Especially small ones. A tiny terrier that charges at bigger dogs is feisty. A cat that hisses and swipes without hesitation is feisty. The word fits perfectly when a small creature acts with the confidence of a much bigger one.

Exchanges and attitudes: You can also describe a debate, an argument, or a conversation as feisty if it was full of energy, sharp remarks, and neither side backed down easily. "It was a feisty exchange between the two politicians."
The Tone: Is It a Compliment or Criticism?

Most of the time, feisty is a compliment — or at least said with admiration. When you call someone feisty, you're usually recognising that they have spirit, courage, and backbone. There's often a note of being impressed.

"She's a feisty little thing — she won't let anyone walk over her."
"Despite being the youngest on the team, he was the feistiest — always challenging the coach's decisions with solid arguments."

However, feisty can occasionally carry a slightly negative or condescending edge, depending on how it's said and to whom. If someone in power calls a person "feisty" in a dismissive tone, they might mean the person is difficult, irritating, or unnecessarily combative. Context and tone of voice matter.
What Makes Feisty Different from Similar Words?

Bold = willing to take risks or speak up. Feisty is more specific — it adds the "scrappy fighter" energy.

Aggressive = likely to attack or start conflict. Feisty is milder and more positive — a feisty person fights back, not necessarily first.

Assertive = clearly stating your needs and opinions with confidence. Feisty is more intense and emotional, with more heat and spark.

Spunky / Plucky = very close to feisty. These all describe courageous, spirited people in the face of odds. Feisty leans slightly more toward the combative and argumentative side, while plucky emphasises bravery, and spunky emphasises lively enthusiasm.

Timid, meek, passive = the complete opposites of feisty.

• "The feisty five-year-old argued with her teacher and refused to sit down." — A child showing unexpected boldness and defiance.
  • "He may be 80 years old, but he's still feisty — he debates everyone at the table and never loses." — Surprising vigour in old age.
  • "She gave a feisty response to the criticism, turning every attack back on her critics." — Spirited and sharp pushback.
  • "That little kitten is feisty — it attacked my hand without a second of hesitation." — A small animal with a big fighting spirit.
  • "The match got feisty in the second half, with both teams arguing every call." — An intense, heated situation.
Feisty means full of fighting spirit, boldness, and energy — especially the kind shown by someone small, young, old, or seemingly at a disadvantage who refuses to be quiet, timid, or pushed around.
6069:
To felicitate someone means to congratulate them — to express joy and good wishes to a person on account of something happy or successful that has happened to them.

Think of it as the formal, ceremonious cousin of the word "congratulate." Both words do the same job, but felicitate carries a more dignified, official weight to it.

When you felicitate someone, you are essentially telling them:

"I am happy for you, and I want to express that happiness to you."

The occasion could be anything joyful — a promotion, a wedding, winning an award, graduating, having a baby, or any personal achievement worth celebrating.

The word isn't cold or mechanical. When you felicitate someone, there is genuine warmth and goodwill in it. You're not just ticking a social box — you are actively wishing the person well and sharing in their happiness.
Where and how it is used

Felicitate is a formal word. You are unlikely to hear it in casual conversation between friends. It lives comfortably in:

  • Official speeches — "The chairman felicitated the award winners at the ceremony."
  • Formal writing — "The organization felicitated the scientist for her groundbreaking research."
  • Public events and functions — where dignitaries or guests of honor are formally acknowledged and congratulated.

It is especially common in South Asian English (particularly Indian English), where it is used very naturally in both formal writing and everyday news reporting. In British or American English, it leans toward being literary or slightly old-fashioned, but is still perfectly correct and understood.
Felicitate vs. Congratulate — What's the difference?

They mean essentially the same thing, but here's the subtle distinction:

  • Congratulate is the everyday, universal word. You congratulate your friend over a text message. You congratulate a colleague in the hallway.
  • Felicitate is the ceremonial, formal word. You felicitate someone at a function, in a speech, in a written tribute, or in a structured public setting.

If congratulate is a warm handshake between friends, felicitate is a formal award or a speech at a podium. Same spirit, different register.

There is a secondary, older usage worth knowing. You can also felicitate yourself, which means to count yourself lucky or to take pleasure in a fortunate situation.

For example: "He felicitated himself on having escaped the disaster."

Here, the meaning shifts slightly — it's not about congratulating another person, but about inwardly rejoicing in your own good fortune or a favorable outcome. This usage is rarer and more literary, but you may encounter it in older texts.
The noun form you'll often see alongside it

The noun form is felicitation (plural: felicitations). This is the act of felicitating, or the expression of good wishes itself.

  • "The team received felicitations from across the country."
  • "He offered his felicitations to the newly married couple."

The plural felicitations works exactly like congratulations — it's a direct, warm expression you offer to someone on a happy occasion.

• "The governor felicitated the athletes who won medals at the national games."
  • "We felicitate you on the completion of twenty-five years of dedicated service."
  • "The college felicitated its top-performing students at the annual prize-giving day."

To felicitate = to formally and warmly congratulate someone on a joyful occasion or achievement, expressing sincere happiness and good wishes toward them.

Whenever you see or hear this word, picture someone standing at a podium, smiling genuinely, and honoring someone else's success in front of others — that is felicitation in its truest spirit.
